title: TA9-18853
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants, XXXX XXXX XXXXX (claimant), and her son XXXXX XXXXX (son), are citizens of Israel, who have made refugee claims under sections 96 and 97 (1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA).
At the time of the hearing the son was fourteen years old. The Board appointed the claimant as the Designated Representative for the son.
The claimant alleges the following:

She married XXXX XXXXX (XXXXX) XXXXXX, 1995; he is black, a Christian, and from XXXXX. Her parents were against the marriage because XXXXX was black. Her father threatened to kill the claimant if she married XXXXX. Her parents forbade her brother and any of her sisters to have any contact with the claimant. She became pregnant and her father demanded that she had an abortion. He used force to try to get her to go to a doctor who would perform an abortion. She refused and called the police and made a complaint against her father.

Towards the end of her pregnancy she advocated and protested against the Ministry of Marriage because they would not acknowledge her marriage. She wrote an XXXXX a newspaper regarding Israel's attitude about interracial marriages and marriages to foreigners.2 Once the XXXXXXXXXX was released her mother "announced that the claimant was dead".

The claimant's parents threatened XXXXX to leave the claimant or they would physically harm him. They called him names; after awhile, he felt that the best thing to do was to leave the marriage so that things would become normal between the claimant and her parents. He separated from the claimant in 1996 and they divorced in 2000.

The claimant believes that she is ostracized in Israel; that Jewish men, "do not think of her as a quality woman because she married and had a child with a black Christian man." She stated that when people would speak to her; "they carried their noses up as if they are addressing dirt." She claimed that people discriminated against her because of her past relationship with XXXXX and having a son of mixed heritage.

She wanted a large family of maybe three or four children. However, she believes "it is impossible for [her] to find true love and happiness in life, living in a country where she and her son has been the object of constant racism and threats."
The claimant left Israel and came to Canada on XXXXXXX, 2009, and made a claim for refugee protection on September 22, 2009.

The Board finds that the claimants have not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground or that they would personally be subjected on a balance of probabilities to a risk to life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or torture upon the return to Israel. As such, the Board finds that the claimants are neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA.
The determinative issues for the claim are credibility, state protection and whether the allegations in the claim amount to persecution.
Certified true copies of the claimants' passports are found in Exhibit R/A-2 and the Board is satisfied that their identities have been established.3

The Board has taken into consideration the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines4 in this matter. All relevant factors, such as the social and cultural context in which the claimant finds herself, along with the issues of the state protection and changing country conditions were examined and guided in respect to the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines.

At the beginning of the hearing, the claimant was asked with her Personal Information Form5 (PIF) in front of her, whether her PIF, including her narrative is true, complete and correct. She responded under oath that it was. a. Credibility

The claimant believed that she is ostracized in Israel, that Jewish men would have nothing to do with her because she had been married to a black man and that her son is of mixed heritage. She testified that when XXXXX left her, it was the "beginning of her nightmare." She stated that in Israel she is seen as "a damaged good to every man in her community". She maintained that "no one wants to be a stepfather to a black boy". She further testified that "the only men who did not mind having a relationship with her were black men, but they were afraid of her parents and so the relationship was never fruitful as even she was very afraid of her father."

She testified that she always wanted a large family of three or four children. She further testified that "it is impossible for her to find true love and happiness in life, living in a country where she and her son have been the object of constant racism and threats."

The claimant stated that she researched as to which country would be give her a better opportunity to live without the prejudice and racism that she has faced in Israel and she determined that Canada would be the best place to get married and raise her son. She testified that Canada was known to be a culturally diverse country, with a large multi-racial population, and zero tolerance for blatant racism, and that racial unity is promoted in the Canadian education system.

However, the Board has two concerns with the claimant's testimony: first, the Board does not question that the claimant is genuine in her belief that she is ostracized in Israel and that she believes that all men will not want to be involved with her because of her past. However, there is no persuasive evidence to establish that she would be ostracized by all men in Israel, and that no men in Israel wants to marry her. Secondly, the Board does not find that her allegations amount to persecution and this will be discussed in detail later on in this decision.

The claimant testified that her parents have accepted the son to a certain extent; but they still make rude and racist comments. For example, her mother would cut the son's hair weekly so that it would not be curly.

The son testified about what his life was like in Israel, how he was ridiculed by other children, and by his grandparents. He testified that his classmates were racist and tormented him and how it was difficult to make friends. He mentioned an incident where children placed a deadly insect under his pillow. He stated that he had to change schools due to the bigotry and racism of the students and teachers. He testified that his grandmother sometimes says mean things about his racial background.

The son further testified that it was the right thing to come to Canada. He is now happy to be going to school and he has made many friends and wishes to stay in Canada. The Board finds the son to be credible and a very impressive young man; however, the Board does not find that the racism he had confronted in Israel amounts to persecution which will be discussed in detail in the next section of this decision. b. Discrimination vs. Persecution

To be considered persecution, the mistreatment suffered or anticipated must be serious, and in order to determine whether particular mistreatment would qualify as "serious" it is necessary to examine what interest of the claimant might be harmed and to what extent the subsistence, employment, expression or exercise of that interest may be compromised. This approach has been approved by the courts, which have equally equated the notion of a serious compromise of interest with a key denial of a core human right.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Handbook, which although not binding, has been considered by the Supreme Court of Canada to be a persuasive authority, provides as follows: No. 54: Differences in the treatment of various groups do indeed exist to a greater or lesser extent in many societies. Persons who receive less favourable treatment as a result of such differences are not necessarily victims of persecution. It is only in certain circumstances that discrimination will amount to persecution.6

This would be so if measures of discrimination lead to consequences of a substantially prejudicial nature for the person concerned, i.e. serious restrictions on his or her right to earn their livelihood and the right to practice religion or access to normally available educational facilities. The Board finds that in the case at hand the claimant and her son are not denied their core human rights.

The Board went on to examine whether the cumulative aspect of the discrimination that the claimant suffered in Israel and whether her fear of future persecution can be justified on "cumulative grounds". As noted in Article 55 of the UNHCR Handbook: Where measures of discrimination are, in themselves, not a serious character, they may nevertheless give rise to a reasonable fear of persecution if they produce, in the mind of the person concerned, a feeling of apprehension and insecurity as regard to his future existence. Whether or not such measures of discrimination in themselves amount to persecution must be determined in the light of all the circumstances. A claim to fear of persecution will of course be stronger where a person has been the victim of a number of discriminatory measures of this type and where there is thus a cumulative element involved.7

The Board considered the events that the claimant and the son mentioned in their testimony and their PIF narratives, which if taken individually do not amount to persecution, but if taken together, may justify a claim to a well-founded fear of persecution. However, the Board finds that the incidents taken together still do not amount to persecution. The incidents of discrimination suffered were not such that the claimant and the son were deprived of all hope and recourse. Although there are problems in Israel, like any other country, the government of Israel generally respects the human rights of its citizens.

Having considered all of the evidence, the Board finds that the claimant and her son have not satisfied their burden of establishing a seriously possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or that it is more likely than not, that they would be subjected personally to a danger of torture or to a risk to life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon their return to Israel. c. State Protection

Whether the analysis is under section 96 or 97(1) of IRPA, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant must rebut the presumption of state protection. In assessing the issue of state protection, the Board is guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. In this regard, the courts have established a number of principles relating to state protection and the Board has applied those principles to the case at hand.

There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens except in situations where there is a complete breakdown.8 To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect that national.9 While the effectiveness of the protection is a relevant consideration, the test is whether the protection offered is adequate.10 The evidence that state protection is not adequate must be reliable and probative, and it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that the state protection is inadequate.11

The claimant must approach the state for protection, providing that state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.12 In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim. Where a state is in effective control to its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that it is not always successful at doing so will not rebut the presumption of state protection.13

A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.14 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of presumption of state protection.15

The burden of proof that rests on the claimant increases with the level of democracy of the state in question. The more democratic a state is, the more the claimant must have done, to exhaust all courses of action open to them to demonstrate state protection was or would not be forthcoming.16 When the state in question is democratic, the claimant must do more than simply show that he or she went to see some members of the police force and that his or her effect were unsuccessful.17 Even where the protective services of the home state have gaps or deficiencies, a claimant who alleges a subjective fear based on criminality must, in the absence of a compelling justification, take reasonable steps to access those services.18

The Board cannot accept the claimant's testimony that Israel is a country where she and her son would be persecuted because she married a black man or that the son would be persecuted because he is of mixed heritage.

Israel is a country committed to tolerance and addressing all manifestations of racism and xenophobia. Israel is a democracy which has a well-developed legislative framework for enforcement of criminal law, including hate laws. Israel focuses on the prevention of racially motivated crimes through the use of comprehensive and complementary strategies, including thorough criminal and administrative tools focusing on the prohibition of public incitement to racist discrimination, violence or hatred; public insults or threats; public denial of the Holocaust; leadership or support of activities carried out by racist groups, political parties and movements; hate speech; criminal offences motivated by hatred.19

Racism is widely defined in the Penal Law 5737-1977 as constituting persecution, humiliation, degradation, a display of enmity, hostility or violence, or causing violence against the public or parts of the population, merely because of their colour, racial affiliation or national ethnic origin. Israel continues to focus on the prevention of racist crimes through education and training. The Israeli Police has introduced educational programs for police officers in order to raise awareness and understanding of the characteristics of minority groups and minorities in Israel. The concept of "equal and suitable service in a multi-cultural society" was set as the annual education target of 2007.20

The Office of the Attorney General in Israel safeguards civil liberties, and has complete independence from any political establishment, and functions as the head of prosecution and advises the government on legislation. This Office investigates all incitements to racism, violence, and hate offenses, and files indictments.21

The National Police are under the authority of the Ministry of Internal Security. The Israeli police are generally effective and police corruption generally is not a problem. The Department for Investigation against Police Officers (DIPO) reviews complaints against police officers and may impose disciplinary measures or recommend indictments. The DIPO hired and trained fifteen civilian investigators in 2008, replacing the police investigators who staffed the former Police Investigations Department, which human rights groups had criticized for lacking the independence necessary for adequate investigation of allegations against police officers.22 The police carried out training programs in coordination with academic institutions and human rights NGOs to promote human rights awareness and cultural sensitivities. The National Police provide mandatory culture classes for all new cadets.23

Since 1971, the government has maintained an Ombudsman, who investigates complaints from every stratum of society, particularly from vulnerable individuals or groups. The Office of the Ombudsman investigated some 7,000 complaints on an annual basis. In 2002, the Ombudsman's Office indicated that investigations were conducted for more than half of complaints and more that 35 percent of all complaints were "found to be justified". Complaints to the Ombudsman can be made in any language, and there is no fee.24

Israel also has laws which forbid harassment in the workplace. In 2007, the government created an Equal Employment Opportunities Commissioner who is responsible for collecting information and hearing complaints from workers concerning instances of sexual harassment and/or discrimination based on gender, sexual orientation, parenthood, religion or race.25 Therefore, if the claimant, were to return to Israel and confront harassment and racism that she alleges happened to her in the past, she could make a complaint to the Equal Employment Opportunities Commissioner.

None of this means that the state of Israel provides perfect protection for all citizens. The documentary evidence does acknowledge that Jews and non-Jews are sometimes subject to various forms of discrimination. No state, including Israel, can guarantee perfect protection. However, as Israel is a democratic country, the claimant has a heavy burden in attempting to show that she should not have been required to exhaust all the resources available to them domestically before claiming refugee status.

The Panel is sympathetic to the claimant's and son's situation; however, the claimant's complaints about the willingness and inadequacy of state protection are not well-founded in light of the above documentary evidence. The Board is satisfied that adequate state protection would be available to the claimant and her son should they return to Israel.

In conclusion, the Board has carefully reviewed and considered all the documentary and viva voce evidence and the submissions of counsel and finds that the claimants are not Convention refugees pursuant to section 96 of the IRPA or persons in need of protection within the meaning of section 97(1)(a) or (b) of the IRPA.
